source_lines.32: In the covariance factor model, write $X=AS+\varepsilon$ with $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$, $q<p$, $\mathbb E[S]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon]=0$, $\operatorname{Cov}(S)=I_q$, $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=D$ diagonal positive, and $\operatorname{Cov}(S,\varepsilon)=0$. Then
source_lines.36: For every orthogonal matrix $R\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$, the transformed loadings and factors $A_R=AR^T$ and $S_R=RS$ give another representation with the same covariance matrix. Thus covariance alone does not identify a unique loading matrix or latent orientation. This is a covariance-model claim; if the factors are additionally required to be mutually independent, the proposition does not claim that arbitrary rotations preserve that extra requirement.
source_lines.50: 1.1 By [F1], bilinearity of covariance gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X)=A\operatorname{Cov}(S)A^T+A\operatorname{Cov}(S,\varepsilon)+\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon,S)A^T+\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=AA^T+D$. [F1, given, algebra]
source_lines.52: 2.1 The transformed factors have mean zero, covariance $R I_q R^T=I_q$, and cross-covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(RS,\varepsilon)=R\operatorname{Cov}(S,\varepsilon)=0$. Also $A_RS_R=AR^TRS=AS$, and $A_RA_R^T+D=AR^TRA^T+D=AA^T+D$. Hence the transformed pair is another covariance factor model with the same covariance. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
